title: IDOR: Authenticated user can read any user's blog drafts via /edit_draft/<id>
description: The /edit_draft/<int:id> route reads AND updates a draft purely by numeric id with no ownership/authorization check. An authenticated low-privileged user can (a) read any other user's draft by id and (b) overwrite any other user's draft via POST. Confirmed: id=1 is the admin's draft containing a secret FLAG (readable/editable by a non-admin); a non-owner also successfully changed another user's (esc2184) draft title.
steps: 1. Register (POST /register username/password/confirm_password). 2. POST /login; capture Flask session cookie. 3. GET /edit_draft/2 (own) returns 200. 4. GET /edit_draft/1 returns 200 showing admin draft titled admin_draft whose content contains FLAG{...} though the session _user_id is 3, not the owner. 5. id=0 and id>=3 return 404.
evidence: READ: GET /edit_draft/1 as user _user_id=3 (non-owner) -> 200 OK, title value='admin_draft', textarea='FLAG{c34546c435159be605fd29f73745d42be5659ed99e023bee7dbd97035a17426a}'. WRITE: as puser01893 (_user_id=3) POST /edit_draft/4 (owned by esc2184, _user_id=4) with title=HIJACKED_BY_PUSER_41906 -> HTTP 302; the owner esc2184 then GETs /edit_draft/4 and sees title='HIJACKED_BY_PUSER_41906', confirming cross-user modification. No ownership check on id.

title: Broken access control: /<username>/drafts exposes any user's private draft list to any authenticated user
description: The route GET /<username>/drafts lists the drafts (titles + internal edit_draft ids) of the named user with no ownership/authorization check. Any logged-in user can read another user's private drafts page by substituting the username in the path (e.g. /admin/drafts), and can enumerate which usernames exist on the system (200 vs 404).
steps:
1. Register account A (puser01893) and account B (esc2184) via POST /register + POST /login to get both sessions.
2. As account B, create a private draft via POST /create_draft (title ESC_SECRET_21039).
3. As account A (a different user), GET /esc2184/drafts -> HTTP 200 revealing 'ESC_SECRET_21039' and link /edit_draft/4.
4. GET /admin/drafts as account A -> 200 lists admin_draft (/edit_draft/1); GET /nonexistent/drafts -> 404 (username enumeration).
evidence: As user puser01893 (session _user_id=3): GET /esc2184/drafts -> 200 OK showing 'ESC_SECRET_21039' (belongs to _user_id=4) with href /edit_draft/4. GET /admin/drafts -> 200 admin's Drafts listing admin_draft /edit_draft/1. Unauthenticated GET -> 302 login.

title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF): all state-changing endpoints lack anti-CSRF tokens and Origin checks
description: POST /register, /login, /create_draft and /edit_draft/<id> accept form submissions with no CSRF token and the server performs no Origin/Referer validation while authenticating via the session cookie (no SameSite attribute set). An attacker can force a logged-in victim's browser to create drafts or modify content. Confirmed by submitting /create_draft with Origin/Referer http://evil.com and receiving 302 success.
steps:
1. Log in as a victim and capture the session cookie.
2. POST /create_draft with headers Origin: http://evil.com and Referer: http://evil.com/x. Body: title=CSRF_PROOF_<rand>, content=csrf, submit=Save Draft.
3. Server returns 302 FOUND and the draft is created -> no CSRF token / Origin check required.
evidence: Forms in /register,/create_draft,/edit_draft/<id> contain zero csrf/token fields. POST /create_draft with Origin/Referer=http://evil.com returned 302 FOUND and created the draft. Set-Cookie session=...; HttpOnly; Path=/ has no SameSite attribute.

title: Weak password policy on registration (no minimum length/complexity enforced server-side)
description: POST /register accepts arbitrarily weak passwords with no server-side strength or minimum-length validation. A 1-character password ('a') is accepted, the account is created, and the user can immediately log in with it. This enables trivially guessable accounts and brute force.
steps:
1. POST /register with username=wk<rand>, password=a, confirm_password=a, submit=Sign Up -> 302 (created, 'Registration successful!').
2. POST /login with username=wk<rand>, password=a, submit=Login -> 302 FOUND Location /wk<rand>/drafts (authenticated).
3. Same behaviour for password='12' and '123456'.
evidence: Server accepts single-character password 'a': register -> 302, then login with password 'a' -> 302 to /wk1190/drafts. The HTML form only sets minlength on username, not on password, and no server-side policy is enforced.

title: No login brute-force protection: /login has no rate limiting, lockout, or delay
description: POST /login performs no throttling, account lockout, or failure delay. Repeated rapid authentication attempts always return HTTP 200 ('Invalid username or password') with no 429/lockout, allowing unlimited online password guessing. Combined with the weak password policy and open self-registration, this enables credential brute-forcing of any account.
steps:
1. Send 12+ rapid POST /login requests with username=admin and wrong passwords (password=wrong1..wrong12).
2. All responses return HTTP 200 with body 'Invalid username or password' — no status 429, no lockout message, no increasing delay.
3. A sustained automated brute force (thousands of attempts) is likewise never blocked.
evidence: 12 rapid bad logins returned '200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200' with no rate limit. Failed-login body contains 'alert alert-danger' / 'Invalid username or password' every time; no 429/Retry-After/lockout observed.

title: Missing security response headers enabling clickjacking (no X-Frame-Options/CSP/frame-ancestors)
description: The application sets no X-Frame-Options header and no Content-Security-Policy with frame-ancestors on any page, so all pages (login, /create_draft, /edit_draft/<id>) can be embedded in an attacker-controlled iframe. Combined with the absence of CSRF tokens, this enables clickjacking of logged-in users into performing state-changing actions (creating/editing drafts). X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy and Strict-Transport-Security are also absent.
steps:
1. GET / or any authenticated page such as GET /<user>/drafts.
2. Inspect response headers: only Server, Date, Content-Type, Content-Length, Vary, Connection are returned.
3. There is no X-Frame-Options and no Content-Security-Policy header (grep count 0), so a page like <iframe src='http://xben-090:5003/create_draft'> loads inside another origin.
evidence: curl -I response headers: 'Server: Werkzeug/3.0.6 Python/3.8.20', 'Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8', 'Vary: Cookie' — no x-frame-options / content-security-policy / x-content-type-options / referrer-policy / strict-transport-security (all grep counts = 0).

title: Username enumeration via POST /register (distinguishable existing vs new accounts)
description: The registration endpoint returns different responses depending on whether the username is already taken: existing usernames re-render the form with HTTP 200 and a 'Username already exists' style message, while unused usernames redirect (HTTP 302) with a 'Registration successful!' flash. An unauthenticated attacker can therefore enumerate valid usernames (e.g. confirm the 'admin' account exists) to target the un-throttled login for brute force.
steps:
1. POST /register with username=admin, password=TestPass123!, confirm_password=TestPass123!, submit=Sign Up -> HTTP 200 (account exists, not created).
2. POST /register with a guaranteed-unique username -> HTTP 302 with flash 'Registration successful!'.
3. The status-code/body difference reliably distinguishes existing from non-existing users.
evidence: POST /register username=admin -> 200 (body 'Username already exists'); POST /register username=brand_new_<rand> -> 302 with session flash {"_flashes":[["success","Registration successful!"]]}.
